title: China and India
bigQuestion: How did ancient China and India explain health and illness, and how do their traditions continue today?

story.title: Practice on a Melon
story.kicker: In ancient India, a young surgeon learns to cut on a melon before touching a patient.
paragraphs: Picture a courtyard in ancient India, shaded by a tree. A young student kneels beside a low table. On it sits a large melon, a few gourds and a leather bag filled with water. Beside them lies a row of small metal tools, cleaned and laid out in order.

The teacher, an experienced surgeon, watches closely. He tells the student to make a straight cut in the melon's skin, not too deep. The student's hand shakes a little. He tries again. The teacher nods and points to the leather bag. Next the student will practice piercing it without spilling water.

This kind of training is described in the Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Sanskrit book about surgery. It tells students to practice on fruits, vegetables and other objects before working on people. The goal is a steady hand and a calm mind. A patient should never be the first thing a new surgeon cuts.

Far to the east, in China, other healers were writing their own great books. They listened to the pulse at the wrist and spoke of qi and yin and yang. Two traditions grew up on two sides of the Himalayas. Both are still practiced today, and both are studied by scientists.
story.think: Why do you think the Sushruta Samhita asked students to practice on melons and leather bags first? What do people practice on today?

lessons.title: The Yellow Emperor's Classic
lessons.mainIdea: The Huangdi Neijing, compiled over 2,000 years ago, is a founding book of Traditional Chinese Medicine that teaches qi and yin-yang.
reading: The *Huangdi Neijing* means the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic. It is written as talks between a legendary ruler, the Yellow Emperor, and his wise advisers. Historians think many authors wrote it, and it was put together around 2,000 years ago or a bit earlier. It is a founding text of Traditional Chinese Medicine, or TCM.

TCM teaches that the body is filled with *qi*, often translated as vital energy or breath. In this tradition, health means qi flows smoothly. Illness means qi is blocked, weak or out of balance. Qi is an idea of the tradition. Scientists have not found a way to measure it.

The Neijing also uses *yin and yang*. These are two opposite but connected forces. Yin is linked with cool, dark and rest. Yang is linked with warm, bright and activity. TCM teaches that health needs a balance of both, like day and night following each other.

words.d: the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, a founding text of Traditional Chinese Medicine
in Traditional Chinese Medicine, the vital energy said to flow through the body
in Chinese thought, two opposite but connected forces that must stay in balance

look.title: Yin and Yang in a Day
look.text: Morning sun warms a village. People wake, work in the fields and talk loudly. By evening the air cools, the light fades, and families rest and grow quiet. Then the next morning begins again.
look.prompt: Which parts of the day match yang, and which match yin? How does this picture help explain the idea of balance?

check.q: What is the Huangdi Neijing?
choices: A founding text of Traditional Chinese Medicine
check.why: The Huangdi Neijing, the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, is a founding TCM text.

check.q: How does TCM describe health in terms of qi?
choices: Qi is the same as blood cells
check.why: TCM teaches that health means qi flows smoothly.

check.q: Which is linked with yang in Chinese thought?
check.why: Yang is linked with warm, bright and activity. Yin is cool, dark and rest.

lessons.title: Five Phases and Meridians
lessons.mainIdea: TCM links the body to five phases and teaches that qi travels along channels called meridians.
reading: TCM also uses the *five phases*: wood, fire, earth, metal and water. Each phase is linked to seasons, colors, tastes and organs. For example, wood is linked with spring and the liver. The phases are said to support or hold back one another in a cycle.

TCM teaches that qi flows through channels called *meridians*. There are twelve main meridians, each tied to an organ. Along them lie specific points. These points are the places where acupuncture needles are placed.

Anatomists have looked for meridians as physical tubes or structures. They have not found them. Scientists see meridians as a map inside the tradition, not as a part of the body you can dissect. TCM practitioners use the map to decide where to treat.

words.d: in TCM, wood, fire, earth, metal and water, linked to seasons and organs
in TCM, channels through which qi is said to flow

look.title: Numbers in Two Traditional Maps
look.cite: As taught in standard TCM and Ayurveda texts; summarized by NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
look.prompt: These numbers come from traditions, not from lab measurements. How is that different from counting bones in the body?

check.q: Which list gives the five phases?
choices: Wood, fire, earth, metal and water
Blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile and air
Vata, pitta, kapha, qi and yin
Heart, lungs, liver, kidney and skin
check.why: The five phases in TCM are wood, fire, earth, metal and water.

check.q: What are meridians in TCM?
choices: Channels through which qi is said to flow
check.why: TCM teaches that qi flows through channels called meridians.

check.q: What have scientists found when they look for meridians as physical structures?
check.why: Anatomists have not found meridians as physical structures.

lessons.title: Reading the Pulse
lessons.mainIdea: TCM doctors feel the pulse at three places on each wrist and also look at the tongue to judge a patient's health.
reading: Imagine a TCM doctor gently placing three fingers on a patient's wrist. She presses lightly, then more firmly. This is *pulse diagnosis*. Diagnosis means figuring out what is causing a health problem. The doctor feels the pulse at three spots on each wrist.

TCM names many types of pulse, such as slippery, wiry or thin. Each type is said to show the state of qi and organs. The doctor also looks at the tongue: its color, shape and coating. Then she asks about sleep, food and mood.

Modern doctors also check the pulse, but for different things. They count the heart rate and feel whether the beat is steady. Studies have found that TCM doctors do not always agree with each other when they read the same pulse. That makes it hard to test pulse types as a way to diagnose disease.

words.d: a TCM method of feeling the pulse at the wrist to judge health
figuring out what is causing a health problem

look.title: Two Doctors, One Wrist
look.text: A school nurse presses two fingers on a student's wrist, watches a clock for 30 seconds and counts 38 beats. A TCM doctor presses three fingers on the same wrist and says the pulse feels thin and quick.
look.prompt: What is each healer looking for? Which result could two people check and agree on more easily, and why?

check.q: Where does a TCM doctor usually feel the pulse?
check.why: In TCM pulse diagnosis, the doctor feels three spots on each wrist.

check.q: Besides the pulse, what does a TCM doctor often look at?
check.why: TCM doctors look at the tongue's color, shape and coating.

check.q: Why is it hard to test TCM pulse types scientifically?
choices: TCM doctors do not always agree on the same pulse
check.why: Studies found TCM doctors often disagree when reading the same pulse.

lessons.title: Acupuncture and Herbs
lessons.mainIdea: Acupuncture and herbal formulas are key TCM treatments; evidence supports some uses and not others.
reading: *Acupuncture* is placing very thin needles into points on the skin. TCM teaches that this helps qi flow along the meridians. In many studies, acupuncture has helped some people with certain kinds of pain, such as low back pain or headaches. But fake needling often helps almost as much, so scientists still debate why it works.

TCM also uses *herbal formulas*. These are mixes of several plants, and sometimes minerals, chosen together. One famous story connects to Tu Youyou, a Chinese scientist. She read an old Chinese text about sweet wormwood and fever. Her team found artemisinin in that plant, and it became a major malaria medicine.

Tu Youyou won a Nobel Prize in 2015. Her work shows that old texts can point to a useful plant. But the medicine had to be purified and tested first. Some herbal products can be contaminated or can interact with other medicines. Always tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbs you take.

words.d: placing very thin needles into points on the skin, a treatment from TCM
mixes of several plants, and sometimes minerals, used together as a treatment

look.title: Tu Youyou Remembers an Old Clue
look.text: An old Chinese text said to soak a handful of sweet wormwood in water and drink the juice. This gave our team the idea to extract the plant at a low temperature, which kept the active substance from being destroyed.
look.cite: Tu Youyou, Nobel Lecture, Stockholm, 2015 (summary of her account of Ge Hong's text)
look.prompt: How did the old text help, and what did scientists still need to do before the medicine was safe to use?

check.q: What is acupuncture?
choices: Placing thin needles into points on the skin
check.why: Acupuncture places very thin needles into points on the skin.

check.q: What did Tu Youyou's team find in sweet wormwood?
check.why: Tu Youyou's team found artemisinin, which became a major malaria medicine.

check.q: What does evidence say about acupuncture and pain?
choices: It helps some people with certain pain, but scientists debate why
It works only on broken bones
check.why: Studies show some help for certain pain, but fake needling often helps too, so the reason is debated.

lessons.title: The Charaka Samhita
lessons.mainIdea: The Charaka Samhita is a classic Ayurvedic book about medicine that stresses diet, daily habits and prevention.
reading: *Ayurveda* is the traditional medicine of India. The name comes from Sanskrit and means knowledge of life. Its oldest great books were written down about 2,000 years ago, from even older teachings. Ayurveda is still practiced by many people in India today.

The *Charaka Samhita* is one of those great books. A samhita is a collection. Charaka's collection focuses on internal medicine, which means illnesses inside the body treated without surgery. It was shaped and edited by several scholars over time.

The Charaka Samhita puts a strong focus on *prevention*, which means stopping illness before it starts. It gives advice on daily routines, sleep, food that suits the season, and a calm mind. It also tells healers to examine patients carefully and treat them with kindness.

words.d: the traditional medicine of India; its name means knowledge of life
a classic Ayurvedic book about internal medicine
stopping an illness before it starts

look.title: A Day Planned for Health
look.text: An Ayurvedic daily plan might say: wake early, clean your teeth and tongue, move your body, eat your largest meal at midday, eat foods that fit the season, and go to bed at a steady time.
look.prompt: Which of these habits would a modern doctor or school nurse also likely recommend? Which ones are specific to Ayurveda's ideas?

check.q: What does the word Ayurveda mean?
check.why: Ayurveda comes from Sanskrit and means knowledge of life.

check.q: What is the main focus of the Charaka Samhita?
check.why: The Charaka Samhita focuses on internal medicine and preventing illness.

check.q: What does prevention mean?
choices: Stopping an illness before it starts
check.why: Prevention means stopping illness before it starts, such as through daily habits.

lessons.title: Sushruta the Surgeon
lessons.mainIdea: The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Indian book on surgery that describes many instruments, procedures and training methods.
reading: The *Sushruta Samhita* is linked to Sushruta, a healer and teacher of ancient India. Like other old texts, it grew over centuries. It is famous as one of the world's earliest detailed books about *surgery*. Surgery means treating the body by cutting, repairing or removing parts.

The book describes many surgical tools, often counted at over 100. Many are shaped like the beaks of birds or the jaws of animals. It also describes more than 300 procedures, from treating wounds to removing stones.

The Sushruta Samhita gives careful advice on training. Students practiced cuts on melons and gourds and practiced stitching on cloth and leather. The book also stresses cleanliness around the patient. It shows that ancient Indian surgeons valued skill, practice and preparation.

words.d: an ancient Indian book on surgery linked to the teacher Sushruta
treating the body by cutting, repairing or removing parts

look.title: What the Sushruta Samhita Describes
look.cite: Counts commonly given in histories of Indian surgery, e.g. Dwivedi and Dwivedi, Indian Journal of Chest Diseases, 2007
look.prompt: What do these large numbers tell you about how much surgery Sushruta's students had to learn?

check.q: What is the Sushruta Samhita mainly about?
check.why: The Sushruta Samhita is famous as an early detailed book about surgery.

check.q: What did students practice cuts on?
check.why: The text says students practiced cuts on melons and gourds before real patients.

check.q: Many Sushruta instruments were shaped like what?
choices: Beaks of birds or jaws of animals
check.why: Many tools were shaped like bird beaks or animal jaws.

lessons.title: Noses and Cataracts
lessons.mainIdea: The Sushruta Samhita describes rebuilding a nose with skin from the face and treating cataracts by moving the clouded lens.
reading: In ancient India, a person could lose part of the nose through injury or as a harsh punishment. The Sushruta Samhita describes a way to rebuild it. The surgeon cut a flap of skin from the cheek, kept it attached at one end, and turned it to shape a new nose. This is an early form of *reconstructive surgery*.

Much later, in 1794, a London magazine reported a similar nose operation performed in India, using skin from the forehead. European surgeons learned from these reports. Today, plastic surgeons still use skin flaps that stay attached to their blood supply.

The text also describes treating a *cataract*, a cloudy lens in the eye that blurs vision. In a method called couching, a needle pushed the cloudy lens out of the way so light could enter. It could help people see some light and shapes. Modern cataract surgery is very different and much safer: the cloudy lens is removed and replaced.

words.d: surgery that rebuilds a damaged part of the body
a cloudy lens in the eye that blurs vision

look.title: Ancient Idea, Modern Hands
look.text: A surgeon in ancient India turns a flap of cheek skin to make a new nose, leaving one end attached. A surgeon today repairs a burn on a child's hand with a skin flap that also stays attached to its blood supply.
look.prompt: Why do you think both surgeons leave one end of the skin attached?

check.q: Where did the Sushruta Samhita take skin to rebuild a nose?
check.why: The text describes a flap of skin from the cheek, turned to form a new nose.

check.q: What is a cataract?
choices: A cloudy lens in the eye
check.why: A cataract is a cloudy lens that blurs vision.

check.q: How is modern cataract surgery different from ancient couching?
choices: The cloudy lens is removed and replaced
It pushes the lens aside with a needle
check.why: Today the cloudy lens is removed and replaced, which is much safer than couching.

lessons.title: The Three Doshas
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda teaches that three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, shape each person's body and health.
reading: Ayurveda teaches that the body is guided by three *doshas*. A dosha is a basic force or quality in the body, in this tradition. The three are vata, pitta and kapha. They are built from five elements: space, air, fire, water and earth.

*Vata* is linked with air and movement. *Pitta* is linked with fire and digestion. Kapha is linked with water and earth, and with steadiness and strength. Ayurveda holds that each person is born with their own mix of doshas, called their nature.

In Ayurveda, illness comes when the doshas fall out of balance. Healers suggest foods, routines, oils and herbs to restore balance. The doshas are ideas of the tradition, like qi in TCM. Scientists have not found a way to measure them, and studies of dosha types have given mixed results.

words.d: in Ayurveda, the three basic forces said to shape the body: vata, pitta and kapha
in Ayurveda, the dosha linked with air and movement
in Ayurveda, the dosha linked with fire and digestion

look.title: Three Ideas of Balance
look.text: A Greek doctor says a patient has too much phlegm. A TCM doctor says the patient's qi is blocked. An Ayurvedic healer says the patient's kapha is too strong.
look.prompt: What do these three explanations have in common? How could a scientist test any of them?

check.q: Which list names the three doshas?
check.why: Ayurveda's three doshas are vata, pitta and kapha.

check.q: Which dosha is linked with fire and digestion?
check.why: Pitta is linked with fire and digestion.

check.q: How do the doshas compare with qi?
choices: Both are ideas of their traditions, not measured by science
check.why: Like qi in TCM, the doshas are ideas of the tradition that science has not measured.

lessons.title: TCM in the Modern World
lessons.mainIdea: TCM is used today in China and around the world, often alongside modern medicine, and is studied by scientists.
reading: Walk into a large hospital in China today and you may find two kinds of departments. One offers modern medicine with scans and lab tests. Another offers TCM with herbs and acupuncture. Many patients use both. This mix is called *integrative medicine*.

In the United States, acupuncture is offered at some clinics and hospitals, often for pain. The National Institutes of Health funds studies of these practices. Some studies show benefits for certain uses. Others show no clear benefit beyond a *placebo*, a fake treatment that can still make people feel better.

TCM herbs can be powerful. Some have caused liver or kidney harm, and some products have been found to contain hidden drugs or metals. That is why it matters to buy from trusted sources and to tell your doctor or pharmacist about every herb or supplement you take.

words.d: using traditional practices alongside modern medicine
a fake treatment, used in studies, that can still make people feel better

look.title: A Health Agency's Advice
look.text: Tell all your health care providers about any complementary health approaches you use, including herbs and supplements. This helps ensure coordinated and safe care.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), Be an Informed Consumer guidance, about 2020
look.prompt: Why would a doctor need to know about herbs a patient takes?

check.q: What is integrative medicine?
choices: Using traditional practices alongside modern medicine
check.why: Integrative medicine combines traditional practices with modern medicine.

check.q: What is a placebo?
choices: A fake treatment that can still make people feel better
check.why: A placebo is a fake treatment used in studies that can still make people feel better.

check.q: Why should you tell your doctor about herbs you take?
choices: It is a legal rule for students
Some herbs can cause harm or mix badly with medicines
check.why: Some herbs can harm the liver or kidneys or interact with medicines.

lessons.title: Ayurveda Today
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda is widely used in India and elsewhere today; studies test its practices, and some products have safety concerns.
reading: Ayurveda is still part of daily life for many families in India. The Indian government has a ministry, called AYUSH, that supports Ayurveda, yoga and other traditional systems. There are Ayurvedic colleges and hospitals. Around the world, many people use Ayurvedic ideas about diet and routine.

Scientists study Ayurvedic plants, such as turmeric. Turmeric contains curcumin, which is being studied for its effects on the body. So far, results are mixed, and turmeric has not been shown to cure any serious disease. This is an example of *clinical trials*, careful tests of a treatment in people.

Some Ayurvedic products have raised safety concerns. A 2008 study led by Robert Saper tested products sold online and found that about one in five contained lead, mercury or arsenic. These are *heavy metals* that can harm the body. Some traditional recipes add metals on purpose. Always ask a doctor or pharmacist before using such products.

words.d: careful tests of a treatment in people to see if it is safe and works
metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic that can harm the body

review.why: TCM teaches that qi flows along meridians.
